items.title: Constitutional Roots under Company Rule (1773-1858)
items.body:
## From trader to ruler

- The **East India Company** arrived in **1600** under a charter of **Queen Elizabeth I**; in **1765** it gained **Diwani rights** (revenue + civil justice) over **Bengal, Bihar and Orissa**, turning from trader to territorial power.

## Landmark Acts of Company Rule

| Act | Key contribution |
|---|---|
| **Regulating Act 1773** | First regulation of the Company; created **Governor-General of Bengal** (Warren Hastings, 1st); Supreme Court at Calcutta (1774) |
| **Pitt's India Act 1784** | **Board of Control** to supervise political affairs → **double government** |
| **Charter Act 1813** | Ended trade monopoly (except tea & China); asserted Crown sovereignty |
| **Charter Act 1833** | Made GG of Bengal the **Governor-General of India** (Lord William Bentinck, 1st); centralised legislation |
| **Charter Act 1853** | Separated legislative & executive functions; **open competition** for the ICS; indefinite Company rule |

- These Acts progressively built the **centralised, law-governed administration** that the Constitution later inherited.
keyPoints: EIC arrived 1600 (charter of Elizabeth I); acquired Diwani of Bengal/Bihar/Orissa in 1765.
Regulating Act 1773 created the Governor-General of Bengal (Warren Hastings) and a Supreme Court at Calcutta.
Pitt's India Act 1784 set up the Board of Control, creating double government.
Charter Act 1833 created the Governor-General of India, with Lord William Bentinck as the first.
Charter Act 1853 separated legislative and executive functions and opened the ICS to competition.
items.mnemonic: Charter Act ladder '1813-33-53' = end monopoly → GG of India → open ICS.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Indian Polity: Historical Background (Company Rule)

items.title: Crown Rule & the Road to Self-Government (1858-1947)
items.body:
## Crown takes over

- After the **1857 revolt**, the **Government of India Act 1858** abolished the Company: the **Governor-General became the Viceroy**, and a Cabinet-rank **Secretary of State for India** (with a 15-member Council) was created.

## Growth of representative institutions

| Act | Distinctive feature |
|---|---|
| **Indian Councils Act 1861** | First inclusion of Indians (non-officials) in legislative councils |
| **Indian Councils Act 1892** | Councils could **discuss the budget** & question the executive |
| **Indian Councils Act 1909** (Morley-Minto) | **Separate electorates** for Muslims (communal representation) |
| **GoI Act 1919** (Montagu-Chelmsford) | **Dyarchy** in provinces (transferred vs reserved subjects) |
| **GoI Act 1935** | **Provincial autonomy**; **Federal Court**; RBI & Public Service Commissions |
| **Indian Independence Act 1947** | Two dominions; Constituent Assemblies empowered to frame constitutions |

- The **1935 Act** supplied much of the **structural framework** of the Constitution; the **1947 Act** made the Constituent Assembly a **sovereign** body.
keyPoints: GoI Act 1858 ended Company rule, created the Viceroy and the Secretary of State for India.
Morley-Minto Reforms (1909) introduced separate electorates for Muslims.
Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms (1919) introduced dyarchy in the provinces.
GoI Act 1935 gave provincial autonomy, a Federal Court and provided for the RBI and PSCs.
Indian Independence Act 1947 created two dominions and empowered their Constituent Assemblies.
items.mnemonic: 'Morley-Minto = Muslim electorates; Montagu-Chelmsford = dyarchy' — both start with M-M.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Indian Polity: Historical Background (Crown Rule)

items.title: The Constituent Assembly — Demand, Formation & Composition
items.body:
## Demand for a Constituent Assembly

- **1928**: **Motilal Nehru Report** — first major Indian attempt at a constitution.
- **1934**: **M.N. Roy** first proposed a **Constituent Assembly**.
- **1935**: Congress officially demanded it; **1940**: conceded in the **August Offer**.
- Finally **constituted in 1946 under the Cabinet Mission Plan** (the **Cripps Mission, 1942** had only promised one after WWII).

## Composition

- Planned strength **389 seats** (292 provinces + 93 princely states + 4 Chief Commissioners' provinces); reduced to **299** after **partition**.
- Members **indirectly elected** by provincial assemblies via **proportional representation + single transferable vote**; princely-state members were nominated by rulers.
- **Elections July 1946**; roughly one seat per 10 lakh people.
keyPoints: Idea of a Constituent Assembly first given by M.N. Roy (1934); Nehru Report was 1928.
Assembly was constituted in 1946 under the Cabinet Mission Plan.
Planned strength 389 seats, reduced to 299 after partition.
Members were indirectly elected by provincial assemblies through proportional representation and single transferable vote.
August Offer (1940) accepted the demand for a Constituent Assembly in principle.
items.mnemonic: Seat drop '389 → 299' = partition took 90 seats to Pakistan.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Indian Polity: Making of the Constitution (Demand & Composition)

items.title: Working of the Assembly & Adoption of the Constitution
items.body:
## Key milestones

- **9 Dec 1946**: first meeting; **Dr. Sachchidananda Sinha** the **temporary President** (Muslim League boycotted).
- **11 Dec 1946**: **Dr. Rajendra Prasad** elected **permanent President**; **H.C. Mukherjee** Vice-President; **B.N. Rau** Constitutional Advisor.
- **13 Dec 1946**: **Objectives Resolution** moved by **Nehru**; passed **22 Jan 1947** — became the basis of the **Preamble**.
- **29 Aug 1947**: **Drafting Committee** formed under **Dr. B.R. Ambedkar** (7 members).

## Committees & final adoption

- **8 major + 15 minor committees**; **11 sessions**. Major chairmen: Drafting–**Ambedkar**, Union Constitution & Union Powers–**Nehru**, States/Provincial/Advisory–**Patel**, Rules–**Rajendra Prasad**.
- Took **2 years, 11 months, 18 days**; cost about **Rs 64 lakh**.
- **Adopted 26 Nov 1949**, came **into force 26 Jan 1950**, with **395 Articles, 22 Parts, 8 Schedules**.
- The original was **handwritten** by **Prem Behari Narain Raizada**.
keyPoints: First meeting 9 Dec 1946; Sachchidananda Sinha was temporary President, Rajendra Prasad permanent President.
Objectives Resolution moved by Nehru on 13 Dec 1946, passed 22 Jan 1947; basis of the Preamble.
Drafting Committee (7 members) under Ambedkar was set up on 29 August 1947.
Making took 2 years 11 months 18 days across 11 sessions, at a cost of about Rs 64 lakh.
Adopted 26 Nov 1949, enforced 26 Jan 1950, with 395 Articles, 22 Parts and 8 Schedules; handwritten by Prem Behari Narain Raizada.
items.mnemonic: '2-11-18' = 2 years, 11 months, 18 days to write the Constitution.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Indian Polity: Making of the Constitution (Timeline & Committees)

items.title: Borrowed Features of the Constitution
items.body:
## A 'bag of borrowings' — with an Indian synthesis

After studying more than 60 constitutions, the makers adapted the best features to Indian conditions. The **structural part** rests largely on the **Government of India Act 1935**.

| Source | Borrowed feature(s) |
|---|---|
| **United Kingdom** | Parliamentary government, rule of law, single citizenship, cabinet system, bicameralism |
| **United States** | Fundamental Rights, judicial review, independent judiciary, impeachment, preamble |
| **Ireland** | Directive Principles of State Policy, nomination to Rajya Sabha, method of Presidential election |
| **Canada** | Federation with a strong Centre, residuary powers with the Union, appointment of Governors |
| **Australia** | Concurrent List, joint sitting of Parliament, freedom of trade & commerce |
| **Germany (Weimar)** | Suspension of Fundamental Rights during emergency |
| **erstwhile USSR** | Fundamental Duties, ideal of justice in the Preamble |
| **South Africa** | Procedure for amendment; election of Rajya Sabha members |
| **Japan** | Procedure established by law |

- These borrowings were **modified**, not copied — Ambedkar defended this synthesis in the Assembly.
keyPoints: Parliamentary system, rule of law and single citizenship are borrowed from the United Kingdom.
Fundamental Rights and judicial review are borrowed from the United States.
Directive Principles of State Policy are borrowed from Ireland.
Federation with a strong Centre and residuary powers with the Union are borrowed from Canada.
Emergency provisions (Germany-Weimar), Fundamental Duties (USSR) and the amendment procedure (South Africa) are other key borrowings.
items.mnemonic: 'UK-US-Ireland' = Parliament - Rights - Directives (the three big pillars).
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Indian Polity: Historical Background / Making of the Constitution (Borrowed Provisions)

items.title: Exam-Precision Facts: Acts, Missions & the 1950 Status
items.body:
## Dyarchy under the GoI Act 1919 - which subjects were Reserved?

Provincial subjects were split into two lists. **Reserved** subjects were administered by the Governor with his Executive Council (not answerable to the legislature); **Transferred** subjects went to Indian ministers responsible to the legislature.

| Category | Subjects |
|---|---|
| **Reserved** (Governor + Council) | **Administration of Justice, Land Revenue, Police**, irrigation, famine relief, press, prisons |
| **Transferred** (Indian ministers) | **Local Self-Government**, education, public health, agriculture, industries |

The 1919 Act also **clearly demarcated central vs provincial jurisdictions** and introduced **bicameralism** at the centre.

## GoI Act 1935 - the structural template

- **Residuary powers** were vested in the **Governor-General** (NOT the federal legislature).
- Provided **reserved seats for women**; established a **Federal Court (1937)**, **provincial autonomy** (abolished provincial dyarchy, introduced dyarchy at the centre), and separated **Burma**.

## The three missions

| Mission | Core proposal (exam trigger) |
|---|---|
| **Cripps Mission 1942** | Dominion status **after** WWII; a Constituent Assembly partly **elected by provincial assemblies + princely-state nominees**; any province **not accepting** the new Constitution could **retain its status / sign a separate agreement** with Britain (a 'post-dated cheque') |
| **Cabinet Mission 1946** | Recommended a **federal government** (Union of provinces + princely states) with **grouping of provinces**; framed the Constituent Assembly. It did **NOT** enlarge the powers of Indian courts or add more Indians to the ICS |
| **Simon Commission 1927-28** | **All-white**, with **no Indian member** -> nationwide boycott ('Simon Go Back') |

## Crown-era landmarks & the 1950 status

- **Charter Act 1813**: ended the Company's trade monopoly **except tea and trade with China**; asserted **Crown sovereignty**; earmarked Rs 1 lakh for education. It did **NOT** place Indian revenues under the British Parliament.
- **Queen Victoria's Proclamation 1858**: disclaimed any intention to **annex Indian (princely) States**, placed administration **under the Crown**, promised religious toleration; it did **not** regulate Company trade.
- **Butler Committee 1927**: examined **relations between the Government of India and the princely States**.
- **Custodian of the Constitution** = the **Supreme Court of India**.
- **Status on 26 January 1950** = a **Sovereign Democratic Republic**. **Socialist** and **Secular** were added only by the **42nd Amendment, 1976**.
keyPoints: GoI Act 1919 Reserved subjects were Administration of Justice, Land Revenue and Police; Local Self-Government was a Transferred subject.
Under the GoI Act 1935 residuary powers were vested in the Governor-General, not the federal legislature.
Cripps Mission (1942) allowed any province not accepting the new Constitution to retain its status or sign a separate agreement with Britain.
Cabinet Mission (1946) recommended a federal government with grouping of provinces; it did not enlarge court powers or add Indians to the ICS.
Charter Act 1813 ended the Company monopoly except tea and China trade and asserted Crown sovereignty, but did not put Indian revenues under the British Parliament.
Queen Victoria's Proclamation (1858) disclaimed annexation of Indian States and placed administration under the Crown.
The Simon Commission (1927) was boycotted because it had no Indian member; the Butler Committee (1927) dealt with Crown-princely states relations.
On 26 January 1950 India's status was a Sovereign Democratic Republic; 'Socialist' and 'Secular' were added by the 42nd Amendment (1976).
items.source: M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity (Historical Background); NCERT; Constitution of India

items.title: For Mains — Evolution of the Indian Constitution
items.body:
## Why Mains asks this (Paper-III, Polity & Governance)

The evolution theme is rarely a bare 'list the Acts' question; examiners want you to **argue how far colonial statutes shaped — and how far the framers departed from — the 1950 Constitution**. Build every answer around continuity vs. break.

| Dimension | What to write |
|---|---|
| **Colonial continuity** | Federal three-list scheme, office of Governor, emergency-type provisions, public-service structure, written exhaustive form — all traced to the **GoI Act 1935** (nearly 2/3 of provisions, incl. 250+ articles, drawn from it) |
| **Democratic break** | Popular sovereignty, universal adult franchise, justiciable Fundamental Rights, secular republic — things no colonial Act gave |
| **Synthesis** | 'Bag of borrowings' from 60+ constitutions, adapted not copied (Ambedkar's defence in the Assembly) |
| **Representativeness** | Indirectly elected, Congress-dominated, League boycott — yet inclusive of all communities, women, minorities (Granville Austin's microcosm) |
| **Criticism / limitations** | 'Lawyer's paradise', too bulky, borrowed, un-Gandhian (no village-republic base), elite-driven |
| **Way forward / relevance** | A 'living document' — basic-structure doctrine lets it evolve without losing identity |

**Data / authorities to quote:** Granville Austin, *The Indian Constitution: Cornerstone of a Nation*; GoI Act 1935 as structural source; Objectives Resolution (13 Dec 1946) → Preamble; Ambedkar's 'Constitution is a vehicle of life' and 'if things go wrong it is because man is vile' speeches; 299 members, 11 sessions, 2y 11m 18d; Kesavananda Bharati (1973) for the living-document point.

**AP angle:** the Constituent Assembly's commitment to linguistic justice fed directly into the demand that produced the first linguistic state — **Andhra (1 Oct 1953)** after Potti Sriramulu's sacrifice — and the States Reorganisation Act 1956; a neat bridge from constitution-making to AP's own creation.

**Use in answers:** open by framing the Constitution as 'an evolutionary, not revolutionary, document'; use a two-column continuity/break mini-table; quote Austin's microcosm line; close with the living-document idea to show maturity. A simple timeline diagram (1773 → 1858 → 1919 → 1935 → 1950) earns easy structure marks.
keyPoints: Frame answers as continuity (GoI Act 1935 structural base) vs. break (sovereignty, FRs, adult franchise).
GoI Act 1935 supplied the bulk of structural provisions — federalism, Governor, emergency, three lists.
Quote Granville Austin (microcosm of a nation) and Ambedkar's Assembly speeches as authorities.
Representativeness critique: indirect election, Congress dominance, League boycott vs. inclusive spirit.
AP angle: constitutional commitment to linguistic justice led to Andhra (1953) and SRA 1956.
Close with the 'living document' idea anchored by Kesavananda Bharati's basic-structure doctrine.
items.source: Granville Austin, The Indian Constitution: Cornerstone of a Nation; M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity; Constituent Assembly Debates
